name: DA14695-00000HQ2
title: DA1469x multi-core Bluetooth 5.2 LE SoC family with system PMU: Arm Cortex-M33 to 96 MHz, 512 kB SRAM, SIMO DC-DC, USB charger
summary: DA1469x is a family of Bluetooth 5.2 Low Energy system-on-chips built round an Arm Cortex-M33 with FPU at up to 96 MHz, with a Cortex-M0+ BLE MAC engine, a sensor node controller and, on DA14699, a motor controller for watch hands. It has 512 kB of retained SRAM (384 kB on DA14691), runs code from external QSPI flash through a 16 kB decrypting cache, and carries a power unit with a SIMO buck converter, supply rails for external parts and a JEITA charger fed from USB. DA14695-00000HQ2 is the DA14695 in the 86-ball VFBGA: charger, LCD controller and QSPI RAM controller, no haptic or LED drivers.
key_figures: Arm Cortex-M33 with FPU and 8-region MPU, 32 kHz to 96 MHz, up to 144 dMIPS
Bluetooth 5.2 Low Energy, -18 dBm to +6 dBm TX, -97 dBm sensitivity, 103 dB link budget
512 kB data SRAM (384 kB on DA14691), 16 kB cache SRAM, 128 kB ROM, 4 kB OTP; no embedded flash, external QSPI flash
SIMO buck DC-DC 2.4 V to 4.75 V, USB charger up to 5.0 V with JEITA
8-channel 10-bit SAR at 3.4 Msample/s; 8-channel 14-bit ΣΔ at 1000 sample/s
USB 1.1 FS device, 3 UARTs, 2 SPI+, 2 I2C, I2S/PCM, PDM, QSPI flash and PSRAM, LCD controller
VFBGA86, 6 mm x 6 mm, 0.55 mm pitch

Its outputs and the LDO rails each take their own capacitor: V30 4.7 µF, V18 22 µF, V18P 22 µF, V18F 0.1 µF, V14 10 µF, V12 10 µF. V14 is wired to VSUP_RF, which has its own 10 µF, and V18F to V18P. operation.text: DA1469x is a family of Bluetooth 5.2 Low Energy wireless microcontrollers with several cores. The application core is an Arm Cortex-M33 with a single-precision FPU and an 8-region MPU, rated up to 144 dMIPS and clocked from 32 kHz up to 96 MHz. Code runs from on-chip RAM or from external QSPI flash through a 16 kB 4-way set-associative cache whose controller decrypts on the fly with no added wait states. Alongside sit a software-configurable BLE MAC engine (a Cortex-M0+ with hardware accelerators that runs the controller stack up to HCI), a sensor node controller that runs uCode to gather sensor data without the CPU, a uCode motor controller for the gear trains of analog watch hands, a crypto engine, a PMU with a SIMO buck converter and LDOs, a JEITA battery charger fed from USB, and analog and digital peripherals.
Compatible with Bluetooth 5.2, ETSI EN 300 328 and EN 300 440 Class 2 (Europe), FCC CFR47 Part 15 (US) and ARIB STD-T66 (Japan).

512 kB of data SRAM with retention (384 kB available on DA14691), 16 kB of cache SRAM with retention, 4 kB of one-time-programmable memory and 128 kB of ROM holding the boot code and the PKI routines that authenticate a flash image. The system RAM is made of eight 64 kB banks.
Optimised low-power modes: extended sleep, deep sleep and hibernation.

A SIMO buck DC-DC converter works from 2.4 V to 4.75 V. Four supply pins can power external devices and stay on while the chip sleeps. The chip runs from Li-polymer, Li-ion, coin cell, NiMH and alkaline batteries. The hardware charger works up to 5.0 V, with programmable charge curves and JEITA support. Brown-out detection thresholds are programmable. On-chip regulators: SYS LDO, RET LDOs, SLEEP LDO, CORE LDO, AON LDO and RADIO LDO.

Digitally controlled oscillators: a 32 MHz crystal oscillator (crystal tolerance ±20 ppm maximum) with an RC oscillator beside it, and a 32 kHz crystal oscillator (±50 ppm, ±500 ppm maximum) with the RCX oscillator beside it. A PLL produces 96 MHz.
The crypto engine does AES-256, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512, and a true random number generator that complies with FIPS 140-2 is included.
A real-time clock with 10 ms resolution and four 24-bit up/down general-purpose timers with PWM.

Up to 55 GPIOs; a QSPI flash interface with decryption on the fly; a separate QSPI PSRAM interface; a parallel or SPI LCD controller with its own DMA; three UARTs to 1 Mbps, one of them extended for ISO7816; two SPI+ controllers; two I2C controllers at 100 kHz, 400 kHz or 3.4 MHz; a PDM interface with a hardware sample-rate converter (two microphones); an I2S/PCM master or slave interface of up to eight channels; and a USB 1.1 full-speed device interface.

The 2.4 GHz transceiver and modem connect to the antenna on one wire, with no RF matching network or RX/TX switch needed. Transmit power is configurable from -18 dBm to +6 dBm and receive sensitivity is -97 dBm, which gives a 103 dB link budget. Current drawn at VBAT2 with an ideal DC-DC converter: 3 mA in TX, 1.8 mA in RX.
An 8-channel 10-bit SAR ADC at 3.4 Msample/s; an 8-channel 14-bit ΣΔ ADC at 1000 sample/s; a haptic driver for LRA and ERM motors; two matched white-LED drivers.
VFBGA86, 6 mm x 6 mm, 0.55 mm ball pitch (DA14691, DA14695); VFBGA100, 5 mm x 5 mm, 0.475 mm ball pitch (DA14697, DA14699).
Smart and sport watches, fitness trackers, keyboards with a rechargeable battery, remote controls driven by voice, toys, consumer appliances, and automation in the home and in industry.

The Cortex-M33 (with MPU, FPU, trace and SWD) reaches memory through the 16 kB instruction cache and its 4-way cache controller, the secure QSPI flash controller, the QSPI RAM/flash controller, the parallel LCD controller, the OTP and boot ROM, and eight 64 kB SysRAM banks. An 8-channel DMA controller, the motor controller, the sensor node controller and the crypto block (AES-256, SHA-1/SHA-2 hash and TRNG) share the system. The BLE 5.x configurable MAC is a Cortex-M0+ with hardware accelerators driving the 2.4 GHz radio transceiver and modem. On the APB sit the communication blocks (UART, UART2, UART3 with ISO7816, SPI, SPI2, I2C, I2C2), the audio blocks (PDM for two microphones, PCM/I2S, sample-rate converter), the analog blocks (14-bit 8-channel ADC2, 10-bit 8-channel ADC, two WLED drivers, LRA/ERM driver, two temperature sensors) and the timers (a 25-bit always-on MAC timer, two pairs of 24-bit always-on PWM timers, RTC, watchdog and wake-up controller), with the USB 1.1 full-speed device controller and PHY and charge detection beside them. Clocks come from the 32 MHz crystal, 32 MHz RC and RCX oscillators, the 32.768 kHz crystal and the 96 MHz PLL; power from the SIMO buck (rail outputs V30, V18F, V18 and V18P), the charger, the LDOs and the brown-out and power-on reset block.

Three system examples. An activity tracker on DA14695/7: magnetometer and light/UV sensors on I2C and SPI, an accelerometer/gyro on SPI, GPS on UART, eight buttons on GPIO, a 144x168 LCD on SPI, QSPI flash, a capacitive touch controller and heart-rate monitor on I2C, a secure element or NFC on ISO7816, an LRA/ERM motor, a white LED, UART debugging and JTAG, USB 1.1, a 32 MHz crystal, and coin cells or a rechargeable battery at 1.8 V to 4.75 V. An analog watch on DA14699: accelerometer/magnetometer and accelerometer/gyro on SPI, GPS on UART, eight buttons on GPIO, QSPI flash, control of 20 hand motors, a secure element on ISO7816, an LRA/ERM motor, a white LED, UART debugging and JTAG, 32 kHz and 32 MHz crystals, USB and coin cells at 1.8 V to 3 V. A sport watch on DA14697: a temperature/pressure/humidity sensor, magnetometer and accelerometer/gyro on SPI and I2C, GPS on UART, eight buttons on GPIO, a 215x215 graphics LCD on SPI, QSPI flash, a digital microphone, a capacitive touch controller and heart-rate monitor on I2C, a secure element or NFC on ISO7816, an LRA/ERM motor, a white LED, UART debugging and JTAG, USB 1.1, a 32 MHz crystal, and coin cells or a rechargeable battery at 1.8 V to 4.75 V. In all of them the external parts take their supply from the DA1469x PMU.

DA14691 and DA14695 come in an 86-ball VFBGA of 6 mm x 6 mm; DA14697 and DA14699 in a 100-ball VFBGA of 5 mm x 5 mm. On VFBGA86, P1_12 to P1_22, the haptic driver and the LED driver pins are absent and balls J4 and K4 are not connected.

Each port pin has a fixed ball, and its further functions are chosen in its Px_xx_MODE_REG. Every port pin has a selectable pull-up or pull-down and an open-drain option. All are pulled down during and after reset except P0_04, P0_10 and P0_12, which are pulled up. All hold their state through power-down except P0_14 and P0_15 (the USB pins). P0_00 to P0_05 are QSPI-type pads, usable as GPIOs at 1.8 V only, with drive selectable among 4, 8, 12 and 16 mA. Pins marked DIO/RDS have a reduced-drive mode of 0.15 mA in place of their 4.8 mA, set in PAD_WEAK_CTRL_REG. SPI, I2C, UART, ISO7816, PCM and PDM signals are mapped onto any port pin (Px_yy); the LCD SPI signals have no fixed ball.

The Cortex-M33 debug port is SWDIO on P0_10 and SWCLK on P0_11; the Cortex-M0+ debug port is SWDIO on P0_12 and SWCLK on P0_13. During boot P0_08 is the UART receive line and P0_09 the UART transmit line. Clock outputs: XTAL32M on P0_12, RC32M on P0_13, XTAL32k on P0_14, DIVN on P0_15, RCX on P0_16 and RC32k on P0_17.

Minimum and maximum limits are covered by design, production test or statistical characterisation; typical figures come from characterisation and are for information. Unless a row says otherwise the conditions are VBAT1 = VBAT2 = 3.0 V and TA = 25 °C, and radio figures are taken with 50 Ω source and load impedance. Capacitor limits are effective capacitance, which falls with applied voltage as the dielectric derates.

The application processor is an Arm Cortex-M33 rated 1.5 dMIPS/MHz, up to 144 dMIPS, running the BLE host and the application and fetching code from QSPI flash through a 16 kB cache; encrypted flash code is decrypted on the fly with no added wait states. The BLE 5.x link layer runs on the configurable MAC (CMAC), a Cortex-M0+ with hardware accelerators. A 128 kB ROM holds the boot code and the elliptic-curve image authentication. The 4 kB OTP keeps the image decryption keys, the application AES keys, the public keys for image authentication and the production trim values, with room for a small secondary bootloader. Up to 512 kB of data RAM, built from 64 kB cells that can each be retained or switched off, is shared by every bus master. There are two QSPI controllers: one for flash with execute-in-place and an AES-256 on-the-fly decryptor, one for PSRAM or a second flash. Other blocks: a parallel and serial LCD controller with its own DMA; AES-256, SHA-1/SHA-2 hash and a true random number generator; a motor controller for coil (Lavet) motors that runs while the rest sleeps; UART (to 1 Mbps), UART2 with hardware flow control and UART3 with ISO7816 (both to 3 Mbps), each with a 16-byte FIFO; SPI and SPI2, master or slave, with an 8-byte RX and a 4-byte TX FIFO; I2C and I2C2, master or slave, each with a 32-place FIFO, up to 2.9 Mbps on a 32 MHz system clock; PDM, sample-rate converter and PCM/I2S audio for two digital microphones or speakers or an external codec; a 10-bit GP ADC with 8 external inputs that oversamples up to 64 times for 11 effective bits; a 14-bit sigma-delta ADC with 8 external inputs and an optional external reference.

The 2.4 GHz radio carries the BLE digital and analog PHY. Four 24-bit general purpose timers (two in the system domain, two in their own domain) give PWM, two capture channels, up/down and free-running counting, a choice of clock and one-shot pulses of set width. The RTC keeps 12/24-hour time down to hundredths of milliseconds, with an alarm and an interrupt on any rollover. The wake-up controller watches any GPIO with a chosen polarity and has one debouncer for a key press. The LRA/ERM haptic driver is an H-bridge that tracks the actuator's resonance, with a settable drive current for the force. Two white-LED drivers sink up to 20 mA each, PWM-dimmed, with current settable to within +/- 5 %. The USB full-speed device (12 Mbit/s, 7 endpoints) serves firmware updates and battery charging. The 8-channel DMA moves memory-to-memory and memory-to-peripheral data in single or burst transfers, and in secure mode carries keys from OTP to the crypto registers without the CPU seeing them. The sensor node controller is a seven-instruction state machine that drives the serial interfaces and moves sensor data straight to RAM.

There are two 13-bit watchdogs. The system watchdog sits in the always-on domain, starts counting down at power-up on its own, raises an NMI at 0 and a hardware reset at -16; its longest period is 84 s on RC32K or 3 minutes on RCX. The CMAC watchdog sits in the radio domain, interrupts the CMAC CPU at 0 and resets at -16. Both stop while either CPU is halted in debug.
The digital logic is split into seven domains, PD_SYS, PD_AON, PD_COM, PD_MEM, PD_TMR, PD_PER and PD_RAD, each switched on and off on its own.

A hardware state machine clocked at 32 kHz runs power-up, wake-up and go-to-sleep. After POR it enters LDO_SUPPLY: COLD_BOOT is set and LDO_VBAT is started; the LDO settles in under 300 µs and the state times out at 400 µs. State BG starts the bandgap and lasts one 32 kHz cycle. State LDO_CORE_RADIO starts LDO_CORE (core at 0.9 V) and LDO_RADIO (V14 at 1.4 V) as POWER_CTRL_REG enables them, timing out at 150 µs. The next two states bring up V18P and V18 if enabled, each with a 300 µs timeout. A last one-cycle state (RAILS_OK) checks every rail, then the machine enters RUNNING and raises WOKENUP, which can be routed to a GPIO or read in a register, and software starts. SYS_STAT_REG[POWER_IS_UP] shows that the domains are initialised.

Slow wake-up repeats the cold-boot states but clears COLD_BOOT; it takes about 1 ms typically and up to 1.5 ms if every state times out, and suits sleeps longer than about four seconds. Fast wake-up starts all LDOs in one state and checks only the core and radio levels, clears COLD_BOOT, takes no more than 300 µs and suits shorter sleeps. Ultra-fast wake-up, about 100 µs, checks no LDO: the CPU runs a couple of low-power clock cycles after the trigger (GPIO or timer) is sampled, while the hardware runs a fast wake-up behind it. Until that reaches RUNNING the CPU should stay at 32 MHz on RC32M rather than the PLL, and external devices fed by the chip should stay off.

Deep sleep is entered only when the power domain controller has nothing pending from any of the three masters. Asleep, two jobs can repeat: the bandgap is woken at an interval of low-power clocks set by BG_REFRESH_INTERVAL in PMU_SLEEP_REG to refresh the reference of LDO_CORE_RET, which holds the sleep voltage, and the BOD samples each rail while the bandgap is on, clocked at 1 MHz from RC32M.

Hibernation (shipping): no RAM kept, no clock and so no RTC, every domain off; only POR, hardware reset or a GPIO wakes it, RC32K must be the low-power clock, and waking resets the system. Deep sleep: no RAM kept, XTAL32K and the RTC run, every domain off; POR, RTC alarm or GPIO wake it. Extended sleep: chosen RAM kept, XTAL32K or RCX running (RTC on only with XTAL32K), every domain off; POR, RTC alarm, MAC timer, another timer or GPIO wake it. Active/idle: running with whichever domains the job needs, for example PD_COM and PD_MEM for the sensor node alone. No CPU state is kept: the CPU always wakes from reset and software restores what it saved in RAM.

Segment 1 of the OTP holds the configuration script, a list of 32-bit words at most 256 deep (1 kB), run by the booter before any application code. It writes registers with production values, stores trim values for software and sets the UART boot timeout.

Three key groups live in OTP: QSPI firmware decryption keys used by the cache path for on-the-fly decryption of execute-in-place code, user symmetric keys used with the AES engine, and public keys for secure-boot image authentication. Each group has an index of eight entries, one per 256-bit key, each starting at 0xFF; writing 0x00 to an entry revokes that key for good. Only the booter revokes keys.
About 2 kB of OTP can hold a small secondary bootloader; address zero can be remapped to the OTP base so the CPU starts there after boot.

Flash is divided into regions, 0.5 MB by default (CACHE_FLASH_REG[FLASH_REGION_SIZE], settable in the configuration script), so several images can sit in one device and the cache controller can map each one. Every image starts on a region boundary; the first region holds the product header, a primary and a backup copy on 4 kB sector boundaries, carrying the programmed identifier, active and update image addresses, the QSPI BURSTCMDA/B values and a flash configuration section (type 0xAA11) with its CRC. An image header carries identifier, size, CRC, a 16-byte version string, a timestamp and the IVT offset, then optional security (0xAA22: ECC key index, symmetric key index, 8-byte nonce), signature (0xAA33) and device administration (0xAA44) sections, the last holding key revocation records (0xAA55) with key type 0xA1 signature, 0xA2 decryption or 0xA3 user data and a key index. 0xFF fills the gap to the image, which starts on a 1 kB boundary. With a device administration section the signature covers that section, the padding and the image; without it, the image alone.

The booter runs after POR, hardware reset, or wake-up with RESET_ON_WAKEUP set. It can boot from cached QSPI flash without security and the script in OTP or in flash, from cached QSPI flash with security and the script in OTP, from UART, or from OTP. It applies pending updates as the flash header says. It cannot boot an image whose product header or active partition lies past the 128-Mbit address (0x1000000), since the opcode for addresses over 24 bits differs between flash makers. The phases are initialisation, configuration script, retrieving the code, device administration and loading the image.

Initialisation starts LDO_RADIO and the power domains, sets up the OTP controller, QSPI and clocks, turns on development mode (debugger on, firmware by UART) so the script can turn it off, clears the XTAL_ok flag and prepares the UART at 115k2 without enabling it. The script is looked for at OTP 0x00000C00 or the start of QSPI flash, found by its start command, and run until a stop command, an empty entry or the length limit. Then XTAL32M is started; if its settle and trim-ready bits come within 10 ms XTAL_ok is set and the clock moves to XTAL32M, otherwise it stays on RC32M. In development mode the booter enables debug and tries UART first; a UART image is run by remapping address zero to RAM and a software reset, and failing that it looks for a flash product header. Out of development mode it needs a valid product header (programmed identifier and active image address). Device administration compares the active and update addresses to find an update; with secure boot set, the image is checked with Ed25519 against a non-revoked public key, with the PLL on and the CPU at 96 MHz, and any key revocation record is then applied by an OTP write. Loading sets up the QSPI and cache controllers, runs the QSPI loader from the product header, decrypts on the fly under secure boot, points the cache at the vector table copied to RAM and remaps address zero to flash. Any error in these phases ends in a hardware reset.

Three processors (Cortex-M33, CMAC, sensor node controller) may want the same peripheral, for instance the GP ADC for both a radio calibration and a battery reading. A hardware mutex settles ownership: the 32-bit BUSY_STAT_REG, changed only through the write-only BUSY_SET_REG and BUSY_RESET_REG so simultaneous writes cannot race. Each resource takes two bits: 0x0 free, 0x1 held by the sensor node controller, 0x2 by the Cortex-M33, 0x3 by the CMAC. The register lives in PD_MEM, on whenever any master is awake, and is lost in deep sleep.

Up to eight 256-bit symmetric keys each for image decryption and for the application, and up to eight 256-bit ECC keys for image authentication, can be stored, and any key in use can be revoked in the field through the booter. Secure boot is set by SECURE_BOOT_REG[SECURE_BOOT] in the OTP script: the booter starts the PLL, runs at 96 MHz, verifies the flash image with Ed25519 and continues only on a match, otherwise it issues a hardware reset. SECURE_BOOT_REG[FORCE_DEBUGGER_OFF] cuts the SWD signals from the CPU's debug port for good; apart from it, SYS_CTRL_REG[DEBUGGER_ENABLE], off after reset, is turned on by the booter while it retrieves the code, so with an empty script the debugger is live a few microseconds after power-up. Each die carries a 64-bit identity written at production test (die position, wafer, package, test time stamp, tester and site). The crypto hardware provides AES up to 256 bits with ECB, CBC and CTR and key expansion, hashing up to SHA-512, and a TRNG giving 1024 random bits in 64k clock cycles.

The PMU has a synchronous single-inductor multiple-output (SIMO) buck with four outputs and a programmable charging order, each output switched on or off on its own; two of its 1.8 V outputs supply up to 50 mA each to external devices. An LDO gives up to 3.3 V at up to 150 mA. LDOs are current-limited in active and sleep. V30, VDD1V8 and VDD1V8P keep feeding external parts while the chip sleeps. A CC/CV charger with battery and die temperature protection, a charger detector and a DC-DC interrupt complete it. Input ranges are 4.2 V to 5.75 V on VBUS and 2.4 V to 4.75 V on VBAT1. The decoupling values given for the rails are nominal: 4.7 µF on VBUS, VBAT1, VBAT2 and V30, 22 µF on V18 and V18P, 0.1 µF on V18F, 10 µF on V14, V12 and VSUP_RF, and 0.47 µH between LX and LY.

VBUS is present while charging from USB. VBAT1 and VBAT2 are joined outside the chip: VBAT1 feeds the LDOs and VBAT2 the SIMO converter. Two clamps and LDO_SLEEP are always powered and hold the supply through extended sleep, deep sleep and hibernation. On wake-up the hardware brings up a set of PMU blocks by itself; software starts the SIMO converter and the rest. The power domain controller switches the digital domains.

One 470 nH inductor serves four outputs: V18P, 50 mA in active, 1.8 V +/- 5 %, for external devices that must stay powered; V18F for the external QSPI flash, with the same figures as V18P; V14, up to 20 mA at 1.4 V, wired to VSUP_RF on the board and not for external loads; V12, the digital core supply, up to 50 mA at 1.2 V in active and not for external loads. The output capacitors are 10 µF on V14 and V12 and 22 µF on V18 and V18P. Switch on-time is not clocked: it ends at a varying inductor current limit. Clocked comparators start a charge cycle when an output falls too low; when several are low together a priority register sets the order, loaded into a four-place shift register. In active mode the current limit is trimmed one LSB at a time: down when an output stays above its minimum too long after a charge, up when it falls back too fast, which keeps ripple low.

LDOs supply the rails while the converter is off (sleep, start-up), on a USB charger, or when VBAT2 is too low for efficient buck conversion (< 2.3 V), with the switch made by hardware or by software. Two retention LDOs, one on VBUS and one on VBAT, feed Vcont and so LDO_SLEEP, a clamp that supplies PD_AON in every mode and can go down to 0.75 V. In sleep, LDO_VBAT_RET feeds the system line, LDO_SLEEP the core and LDO_IO_RET/LDO_IO_RET2 the external 1.8 V rails; the radio supply is off in every sleep mode. The three retention types (VBAT, core, IO) share one sample-and-hold design: a held reference capacitor leaks, so the bandgap is started every BG_REFRESH_INTERVAL sleep-clock ticks to refresh it and then stopped. In active with a 1.7 V to 2.4 V supply and the converter bypassed, LDO_VBAT feeds Vsys, LDO_IO/LDO_IO2 the 1.8 V rails, LDO_CORE the core and LDO_RADIO the radio. On USB, LDO_USB feeds the system line instead, switching on by itself once VBUS > VBAT1.

The converter may start whenever one of the masters (M33, M0+, SNC) is on; no master turns it off. When the system goes to sleep the converter stops because its state machine is in PD_MEM. Hardware never starts it: software sets DCDC_CTRL1_REG[DCDC_ENABLE] and then the wanted DCDC_Vxx_ENABLE_xV output bits, and the LDO and retention LDO on that rail are then turned off by hardware, so a rail never has two drivers. After wake-up the state machine brings the LDOs back as POWER_CTRL_REG sets them, and the DC-DC registers are reset.

Clamps, not regulators, feed V30 and V12 at light load. The V30 clamp follows VBAT or VBUS less a threshold and gives enough current to start the bandgap during power-up. The V12 clamp keeps the always-on logic alive in hibernation without bandgap or retention LDOs; it is programmable and can be lowered in hibernation.

BATCHECK loads VBAT with a programmable constant current of 0 to 8 mA in 1 mA steps, accurate to +/-2.7 %, so the battery's internal resistance can be measured. A bandgap reference current is mirrored to the chosen value, dropped across a resistor and copied by a high-gain op-amp and output transistor onto a matched resistor. BATCHECK_REG holds the setting, fine trim and enable.

DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699 have the charger; DA14691 has none. It charges NiMH, Li-phosphate, Li-Co, Li-Mn and NMC cells through an internal pass device, needing only a buffer capacitor and an NTC outside. It is CC/CV with battery and die temperature protection: charge voltage 2.8 V to 4.9 V, charge current 5 mA to 560 mA, or 0.5 mA to 56 mA in pre-charge. A hardware state machine runs enabling, disabling and the states; software handles exceptions and errors and may take over at any point, but charging needs no timed software. Current, voltage and temperature loops and protections are all hardware, and VBAT and battery temperature are measured without the ADCs. Status signals report the CC or CV phase, die over-temperature, battery hot, cold or OK, and end of charge (current below 10 % of the setting). The states are disabled, pre-charge, CC, CV, end of charge, die temperature protection, battery temperature protection and error, with a bypass for software control; recharge starts when VBAT falls below VCHARGE - VREPLENISH.

Following JEITA, full charge current and voltage apply in the normal range, reduced current (and optionally voltage) in a warm and a cool band on either side, and no charging when very hot or very cold. The pack NTC sits in series with an external resistor R1: P1_00 drives the pair as NTC supply and P0_07 reads the middle as NTC input. The divider voltage is compared with a programmable resistor ladder that copies the NTC curve, with taps about every 1 °C from -10 °C to +55 °C. For this use both pins are set as GPIO (Px_yy_MODE_REG[PID] = 0), P1_00 as an output driven high and P0_07 as an input with no pull. A monitor state machine checks hot, cold, warm, cool and normal in turn, once or on CHARGER_TBAT_MON_TIMER_REG, and applies the current and voltage settings of the zone found.

Detected: pre-charge, CC, CV and total charge timeouts, battery over-voltage, die over-temperature (a flag, not an error state), battery too hot or too cold, and VBUS removed. Voltage and temperature errors open the charge loop directly. A timeout, over-voltage or VBUS fault sends the state machine to ERROR, disables the charger and raises an interrupt whose status register names the cause.

DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699 have it; DA14691 does not. The USB block identifies the port type so the right current can be drawn: BC1.2 (Revision 1.2, December 7, 2010) dedicated charging port, charging downstream port, standard downstream port, PS2 port and proprietary chargers, with dead battery provision and smartphone charger support. Its parts: a 0.6 V source switchable to USBP or USBN (VDP_SRC_ON, VDM_SRC_ON); a 100 µA sink switchable to either line, never both (IDP_SINK_ON, IDM_SINK_ON); a 10 µA source IDP_SRC with the 15 kΩ RDM_DWN (IDP_SRC_ON); Schmitt inputs read as USB_DP_VAL and USB_DM_VAL (0 below 0.8 V, 1 above 2 V); comparator CHG_DET for 0.4 V < USBN < 1.5 V (DCP or CDP) and DCP_DET for 0.4 V < USBP < 1.5 V (DCP). USB_CHARGER_CTRL_REG starts at all zeros; BAT_STATUS_REG[VBUS_AVAILABLE] shows VBUS. It works by polling or by a USB interrupt: a change in bits [3:0] of USB_CHARGER_STAT_REG sets USB_MAEV_REG[USB_CH_EV] where bits [7:4] allow it, and reading the status register clears it, a new set winning over the clear. For contact detection software waits out the contact bounce before reading. The smartphone detector is enabled by USB_CHARGE_ON and reports in USB_CHARGER_STAT_REG.

Software can discharge the external decoupling capacitors through NMOS switches by writing DISCHARGE_RAIL_REG, so external parts can be power-cycled on reset. Each rail has a fixed discharge current: 20 mA on V14, VDD1V8 and VDD1V8P, 2 mA on VDD1V8F.

The PDC is a hardware state machine that acts after wake-up and before sleep. Following a programmable look-up table it decides which power domains to start for a wake-up trigger, whether to start XTAL32M, and whether the system may enter deep sleep (DC-DC, bandgap and LDOs off). Triggers come from any GPIO, the general purpose timers, RTC, MAC timer, motor controller, VBUS, SWD presence, internal diagnostics, or software on any of the three masters. It keeps a domain on while any master uses it and lets the system deep-sleep only when every master's domain is off; PMU_CTRL_REG can override wake-up.

An entry's action bits can start XTAL32M (the PDC only starts it; any master may switch the system clock to it and none should switch back; it stops by itself in deep sleep), start PD_TMR or PD_PER (the only domains with no master; PD_MEM is always on while any master runs), start PD_COM (needed by anyone using GPIOs, since it holds the GPIO mode settings), and wake a master. The PDC re-evaluates on every trigger and every time a master reports done: the Cortex-M33 or CMAC by setting SCR deep-sleep and executing WFI, the SNC by its SLP instruction. A trigger sets the entry's bit in PDC_PENDING; the woken master acknowledges it early, well before its own SLP/WFI, and on finishing drops its request. A domain is shut only when no other active entry uses it, and when no entry with a running master remains the system may deep-sleep, each domain going off as PMU_CTRL_REG allows (for example RADIO_SLEEP = 1). Setup: write PDC_CTRLx_REG with TRIG_SELECT (0 GPIO on port 0, 1 GPIO on port 1, 2 peripheral IRQ, 3 another master), TRIG_ID, the EN_COM, EN_PER, EN_TMR and EN_XTAL options and PDC_MASTER (0 entry off, 1 Cortex-M33, 2 CMAC, 3 SNC); read PDC_PENDING_REG; trigger by software with PDC_SET_PENDING_REG; clear with PDC_ACKNOWLEDGE_REG.

The BOD resets the chip when a monitored rail drops below its level. It watches seven rails (VBAT, V30, V18, V18P, V18F, V14 and VDD) separately, each with its own enable in BOD_CTRL_REG and level in BOD_LVL_CTRLx_REG, and works in active, sleep and deep sleep. Asleep it wakes every PMU_SLEEP_REG[BOD_SLEEP_INTERVAL] low-power clocks, compares for one low-power clock period and sleeps again. All detectors are off at start-up. Rails are checked one after another, so each added rail slows the round. The BOD state machine runs at 8 MHz in active and 1 MHz in sleep, and BOD_CTRL_REG[BOD_CLK_DIV] can slow it further at the cost of missing short dips. Setup: set the interval, the levels, then the enables.

RSTn is active low, with an internal spike filter of 400 kΩ and 2.8 pF and a 25 kΩ pull-up; drive it with a FET or a push-button to ground. Its typical latency is about 2 µs. There are three resets. Power-on reset comes from the internal VDD threshold, from the brown-out state machine (including VBAT < 1.6 V), or from RSTn or a chosen GPIO (selectable polarity) held for the programmable POR time. Hardware reset comes from RSTn held for less than the POR time, the watchdog, a debugger request (SWD_RESET_REG[SWD_HW_RESET_REQ]), or automatically on wake-up from extended or deep sleep with PMU_CTRL_REG[RESET_ON_WAKEUP]. Software reset is SYS_CTRL_REG[SW_RESET] or AIRCR[SYSRESETREQ] (SCB->AIRCR = 0x05FA0004), used mainly to restart after remapping. POR and hardware reset run the cold start-up and the boot ROM. The reset cause is latched in a register.

RSTn can always produce a POR; a GPIO can also be chosen with POR_PIN_REG[PIN_SELECT] (0 turns the GPIO source off) and POR_PIN_REG[POR_POLARITY] (0 active low, 1 active high), and keeps working as a GPIO. A source held starts the POR timer and releasing it early clears the count; if a second source is asserted before the first is released, POR happens once the two together have been held for POR_TIME. The timer runs on RC32K, which hardware restarts if software stopped it (the watchdog shares it); from RSTn RC32K uses its reset trim, from a GPIO its programmed trim. PIN_SELECT is cleared by every reset and POR_TIME by POR, so software sets them again after reset. A GPIO POR source adds about 100 nA, in sleep as well, for the running RC32K; RSTn adds nothing. Default time is about 3 s (POR_TIME = 0x18), longest about 16.2 s at 25 °C. RC32K runs 23 kHz to 37 kHz over -10 °C to 50 °C, which sets the spread of the POR time.

The application CPU implements Armv8-M with the Main Extension, floating-point, DSP and debug extensions, an in-order pipeline, Thumb-2, big or little endian data, the NVIC, and a Micro Trace Buffer. Its single-precision FPU has fused multiply-add, hardware divide and square root, denormals and every IEEE 754-2008 rounding mode, 32 single or 16 double registers and lazy context save. It connects by C-AHB, S-AHB, the external PPB (APB) and D-AHB. It loses its state in any sleep that powers its domain off and always wakes from reset; software restores the state. There are 40 interrupt lines besides the NMI.

The cache speeds up and saves power for Cortex-M33 code run from QSPI flash, loading code and data into its data RAM on read. It covers up to 32 MB from the QSPI base in steps of 64 kB; size is configurable, 16 kB by default, with a 4 kB TAG RAM; lines of 8, 16 or 32 bytes and 1, 2 or 4-way associativity, with pseudo-random (LFSR) replacement for 2 and 4 ways. There is no write path, and a bypass mode. Hits cost no wait on the same line and one wait on a new line; a miss costs 4 + (line size / 4) cycles; transparent bypass costs none. Setting CACHE_CTRL1_REG FLUSH invalidates the TAG memory, halting the Cortex-M0+ meanwhile. Data and TAG memory can be read on the AHB system bus for debugging, and data RAM can instead hold code copied from flash.

Addresses 0 to 0x1FFFFFFF are cacheable: with REMAP_ADR0 = 0x1 or 0x2, addresses 0 to CACHE_LEN are cached, otherwise bypass is automatic; CACHERAM_MUX = 0 forces bypass everywhere. CACHE_LEN applies only to the flash remap set in CACHE_FLASH_REG. Line size (CACHE_LNSIZECFG_REG) and associativity (CACHE_ASSOCCFG_REG) can be rewritten at any time with no wait state and no flush; contents survive except when associativity is cut, which typically hides half the data. Physical lines are 8 bytes, a 16 or 32-byte line using 2 or 4 of them, and a new size takes effect as lines are replaced. The memory is four banks, used as 4 ways or joined for 2 or 1. Ways fill from way 0 to way 3, then an LFSR picks the victim. A hardware reset clears the logic, TAG memory and every CACHE_*_REG, clearing the TAGs in about 450 AHB cycles with wait states for any fetch meanwhile; a software reset clears the state machine and TAGs but keeps the registers.

In active mode a monitor counts cache hits and misses over an interval of up to 10 ms (CACHE_MRM_TINT_REG, in CPU clocks) and interrupts the CPU at programmable miss, hit or time thresholds, so software can change line size, associativity or start the PLL. Results are in CACHE_MRM_HITS_REG and CACHE_MRM_MISSES_REG. Setup: stop the counters (MRM_START = 0), set CACHE_MRM_MISSES_THRES_REG, CACHE_MRM_HITS_THRES_REG and CACHE_MRM_TINT_REG, unmask with MRM_IRQ_MASK, choose the interrupts, set MRM_START and read the counts.

Clear CACHE_CTRL2_REG[CACHE_LEN] to disable; program the cache RAM size (CACHE_RAM_SIZE_RESET_VALUE in CACHE_CTRL_3_REG); choose the line size (CACHE_LNSIZECFG_REG, 8 B after reset) and associativity (CACHE_ASSOCCFG_REG, 4-way after reset); flush with CACHE_CTRL1_REG[CACHE_FLUSH]; enable with a non-zero CACHE_LEN. CACHE_LEN other than 1 gives the cacheable flash size; CACHE_LEN = 1 takes it from CACHE_FLASH_REG[FLASH_REGION_OFFSET].

A multi-layer AMBA bus runs transfers in parallel. AHB-CPUC, mastered by the cache, carries code from 0x00000000 to 0x1FFFFFFF. AHB-CPUS, mastered by the Cortex-M33, covers 0x20000000 to 0xDFFFFFFF and above 0xE0100000. AHB-DMA has RFMON, the general DMA, the LCD controller and AES/HASH as masters. Interconnect multiplexers let both AHB sides reach the QSPI flash and QSPI RAM controllers, the 32-bit APB peripherals, the RAM controller, the OTP controller and the AHB register file. Peripheral-to-memory DMA, M33 data and M33 code from flash can all move at once, and the sensor node, DMA, CMAC and M33 can use different memory segments without collision. The APB32 has four possible masters (SNC, CMAC, M33, DMA), with a multiplexer between the sensor node and the bridge. Two protection units guard the security boundary: the OTP protection unit admits access to the OTP key area only over a secure channel, and the flash-register protection unit keeps the CPU from writing the write-only QSPI AES key registers or reading the AES/HASH registers, letting only the DMA through on an active secure channel; both follow the sticky protection bits. AHB-DMA arbitration is programmable since the LCD DMA can hold the bus continuously.

The CMAC is a Cortex-M0+ based MAC that can be programmed for several protocols. It runs code from system RAM with zero wait states (size and base address of its RAM configurable) and reaches every APB peripheral. It carries the BLE 5.x controller with HCI and the optional 2 Mbps PHY, advertising extensions, channel selection algorithm #2, periodic advertising and high duty cycle non-connectable advertising; advertising and keep-alive connections and its own sleep cycles run without the main CPU, with fast wake-up and sleep. Hardware accelerators: link layer and framing timers, AES-128, a 7-bit whitening engine and 24-bit CRC to the BLE standard, a 32-bit correlator, AoA/AoD support and a coexistence interface. A bit-stream controller does the real-time work; the link layer timer schedules radio transactions written to the CMAC registers, which hardware runs at the set moment. Both CPUs can reach the radio and CMAC sleep-timer registers, normally only the CMAC does. Toward the Cortex-M33 the CMAC is the BLE link layer behind an HCI, talking through interrupts and shared RAM with a mailbox.

The SNC is a small hardware state machine with a short instruction set for driving communication controllers and their sensors without waking the rest of the system: polling status bits, comparing registers with memory, moving data from the interfaces to RAM and branching. Its microcode and data are in system RAM, reached through a direct memory port; it is an AHB master in PD_COM with the interfaces and the sigma-delta ADC, can control other domains on APB32, starts as soon as its domain powers up with an interrupt pending, and runs at the system clock or slower. When done it tells the PDC, which may power everything down. Because it can run beside the system CPU, the CPU checks the busy status register before touching a communication interface. It contains the instruction state machine with an 8-bit delay timer, the memory interface, an AHB master for the peripheral registers, an APB32 slave for its configuration (set up by the Cortex-M33, including microcode and buffer base addresses) and a register file with the current opcode and program counter for debug.

When the low-power clock is the system clock, the SNC clock must equal it: a divided SNC clock can upset DEL. For this, HCLK_DIV and PCLK_DIV in CLK_AMBA_REG and SNC_DIV in CLK_COM_REG are each set to 0. Setup: load the code into RAM (a macro library covers the interfaces), set the divider CLK_COM_REG[SNC_DIV] and SNC_BASE_REG, then run it from a PDC entry, or by hand: set SNC_CTRL_REG[SNC_SW_CTRL] to block PDC triggering, set SNC_CTRL_REG[SNC_EN], and watch SNC_STATUS_REG[SNC_DONE_STATUS] (0 running, 1 finished).

The memory controller shares the 512 kB RAM (384 kB on DA14691) among the M33, CMAC, sensor node, general DMA and LCD controller, through AHB ports for the DMA and the system CPU and memory ports for the sensor node, the CMAC and the MTB. Segments are fully programmable so the RAM is not fragmented, and masters working in different RAM cells proceed in parallel without wait states. Where segments share a cell, hardware arbitration gives wait states to the lower-priority master; moving segment boundaries removes them at some cost in fragmentation. The AHB masters (M33, LCD, DMA) stall on HREADY and the sensor node on MREADY; the CMAC and MTB have no stall input, and the CMAC always has the highest priority. Arbitration is static priority from MEM_PRIO_REG (one field per AHB layer and one for the sensor node) or, when MEM_STALL_REG is non-zero, round robin, where a master stalled that many cycles takes top priority.

A suggested layout of the eight 64 kB cells (0x00000 to 0x80000): the vector table at the bottom of RAM 1, about 300 kB of application data up through RAM 5, about 135 kB of CMAC stack code and data into RAM 7, an 8 kB mailbox, 12 kB left empty, then in RAM 8 40 kB of sensor node data, 4 kB of sensor node code and the 8 kB MTB trace buffer at the top. Only RAM 8 is fragmented. The MTB, which cannot stall, takes top priority there, and the CMAC, which cannot stall either, must not share a cell with the MTB. Other cells can be shared at the price of wait states, or busy users can be put in separate cells at the price of empty gaps.

Three main clocks. lp_clk, the sleep clock, is RCX, RC32K or XTAL32K (CLK_CTRL_REG[LP_CLK_SEL]). sys_clk drives hclk for the CPU, memories and bus and comes from XTAL32M, RC32M, the PLL (96 MHz, or divided by 2) or the low-power clock (CLK_CTRL_REG[SYS_CLK_SEL]), or an external digital clock. divn_clk changes its divider by itself to stay at 32 MHz, so the PLL can be switched in for the CPU without disturbing 32 MHz blocks. HCLK_DIV and PCLK_DIV divide hclk and the APB clock; the peripherals have their own enables, selects and dividers (SPI, I2C, UART, GPADC, LCD, SRC, PDM, PCM, motor controller, QSPI and QSPI2, timers, SNC, CMAC). RC32K or RCX divided by a fixed 320 clocks the watchdog; the BOD clock is divided by 8 and BOD_CLK_DIV. The PLL with sys_clk divided by 2 must not be used while peripherals are accessed, since the APB clock becomes a multiple of 48 MHz while the blocks run on 32 MHz; without peripheral access the CPU may run at 48 MHz.

Two digitally controlled crystal oscillators: XTAL32M at 32 MHz, which can be trimmed, and XTAL32K at 32.768 kHz, untrimmed, the extended-sleep clock. Only the crystal is needed outside; a crystal with a case pin should have the case grounded. The 32 MHz oscillator has on-chip variable load capacitance of 5.4 pF to 11.5 pF. CLK_FREQ_TRIM_REG[XTAL32M_TRIM] sets two capacitor banks together: 0x2BF is the most capacitance and lowest frequency, 0x000 the least and highest; its ten low bits switch ten binary-weighted capacitors.

RC32M gives 32 MHz once trimmed and runs from the digital LDO VDD; untrimmed it is much slower, and it clocks the CPU and logic during power-up and wake-up while XTAL32M settles. RC32K, about 32 kHz (23 kHz to 37 kHz over temperature), runs on VDD and clocks the power-up state machine, the watchdog when chosen, and the POR timer. RCX, about 15 kHz, is better than 500 ppm and steady over temperature, and can replace the 32.768 kHz crystal.

The XTAL32K and RC oscillator frequencies are measured against the DivN clock with an on-chip reference counter: write N to REF_CNT_VAL (larger N, longer and more accurate), choose the clock in CLK_REF_SEL_REG[REF_CLK_SEL], set REF_CAL_START, wait for it to clear and read M from CLK_REF_VAL_REG. With RCX as the sleep clock, calibration is repeated often enough to keep BLE connections.

The low-power PLL multiplies XTAL32M to 96 MHz and locks within a few µs; the system clock can be moved to it on the fly. It gives the 48 MHz (divided by 2) that the USB controller needs and lets the CPU reach 144 dMIPS.

The OTP controller runs the 4 kB OTP: reading, which is transparent to the CPU, and programming, which is not. It has one AHB slave for its registers and one for the memory, runs on the AHB clock and keeps cell accesses at no more than 20 MHz from tick counts in its registers. The cell holds 1024 words of 32 data bits plus 6 ECC bits made and checked inside the cell and never visible; a word reads in one clock. Programming goes one word at a time through a single-word buffer, no bursts; blank words read 0xFFFFFFFF and only zero bits are programmed, plus 6 pulses for the ECC every time. The cell is fed from V30 (1.62 V to 3.63 V) through a power switch the controller drives. Three address ranges are write-protected by the sticky protection bits.

Enable the clock with CLK_AMBA_REG[OTP_ENABLE], select standby and wait for OTPC_STAT_REG[OTPC_STAT_MRDY], and write the timing registers for the bus clock. To program: select mode 0x4 and wait for MRDY, check OTPC_STAT_PBUF_EMPTY, write the data to OTPC_PWORD_REG and the address to OTPC_PADDR_REG, wait for OTPC_STAT_PRDY, change to verify mode 0x5, read back and compare, and return to standby. To read: select mode 0x3, read, and return to standby, waiting for MRDY after each mode change.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. The QSPIC connects a serial flash over single, dual or quad SPI, master only, clock modes 0 and 3, at up to 96 MHz. In auto mode the flash is mapped into memory for execute-in-place and data reads, up to 32 MB with 3-byte or 4-byte addresses, working with the cache in single or burst accesses, with an optional special read instruction for a programmable wrapping burst. In manual mode software drives the flash through the register file, so any flash instruction can be issued. An instruction sequencer makes it independent of the flash vendor; it runs erase suspend/resume so the flash can hold code and data, decrypts AES-256-CTR on the fly in auto mode, and has a hardware state machine that replays microcode commands to the flash on wake-up.

QSPI_SCK is the clock output and QSPI_CS the active-low chip select. QSPI_IO0 is data out in single mode and bidirectional IO0 in dual/quad; QSPI_IO1 is data in in single mode and IO1 in dual/quad; QSPI_IO2 is a general purpose output (for example WPn) in single mode and IO2 in quad; QSPI_IO3 is IO3 in quad and a general purpose output (HOLDn, say) in single mode. QSPI_GP_REG holds the pad settings: QSPI_PADS_DRV for drive strength, QSPI_PADS_SLEW for slew rate. The controller drives every data line except during a read, so the lines are never left floating; turning the pads round takes at least 1.5 QSPI_CLK periods. The IO lines idle at 1 as soon as the controller clock is on; values written to QSPIC_IOx_DAT and QSPIC_IOx_OEN reach the pins only once QSPI_CS goes low.

Because the flash may be powered off or in deep power-down during sleep, the controller can bring it back before the CPU wakes: a hardware state machine decodes commands from a retained 16-word by 32-bit memory and sends them to the flash, handshaking with the PMU by request/acknowledge. The CPU fills this memory at cold boot from the flash header; it starts at address 0x38000040. Each record's wait count is in RC32M cycles (about 32 MHz), at most 4 ms; a flash needing longer gets the same command repeated.

operation.topic: QSPI flash controller SPI and access modes
operation.text: Single mode uses two one-way data pins, dual two and quad four bidirectional pins; the single mode talks to any single, dual or quad flash but has no bus modes 1 and 2, no full duplex and no slave mode. Auto and manual mode exclude each other. QSPIC_CTRLMODE_REG[QSPIC_USE_32BA] = 0 gives 3-byte addressing, up to 16 MB; 1 gives 4-byte addressing, up to 32 MB.

operation.topic: QSPI flash controller auto and manual mode
operation.text: With auto mode off, accesses to the mapped space are ignored. With it on, reads are turned into flash commands transparently and a write causes a hard fault. Single reads, incrementing bursts and wrapping bursts are served; wrapping works even on a flash with no wrap instruction, and one with a wrap instruction needs fewer wait states. Bursts use the bus best; random reads cost more wait states. In manual mode the register file issues any flash instruction and sets the bus width and the mode, with 8, 16 and 32-bit accesses. The controller is little-endian: the least significant byte goes first on 16 and 32-bit transfers.

To store data in the flash, code must run from RAM or the cache while a sector is erased. A hardware state machine handles it: setting QSPIC_ERASE_EN with the sector address in QSPIC_ERS_ADDR requests the erase; once reads have stopped for QSPIC_ERSRES_HLD AHB cycles it sends the write-enable and erase instructions and starts QSPIC_RESSUS_DLY. While the erase runs, a status check (forced by writing the check-erase register) or an AHB read makes it read the flash status after QSPIC_RESSTS_DLY (SPI clock cycles) or QSPIC_RESSUS_DLY (an internal 222 kHz clock), chosen by QSPIC_STSDLY_SEL. If the erase is done it returns to normal and clears QSPIC_ERASE_EN. If a read arrives first, it sends the suspend instruction, polls until the flash is ready, serves the reads, and after QSPIC_ERSRES_HLD idle AHB cycles sends resume and goes back to waiting. Since QSPI_RESSTS_DLY is counted in QSPI_CLK cycles, it is checked against the flash's timing before QSPI_CLK is changed.

In auto mode only, data read from an address range set by ENC_START_ADDR and ENC_END_ADDR (aligned to 1024 B) is decrypted as it is fetched; addresses outside are read as they are. The flash contents must be encrypted with the same scheme: AES in CTR mode with a 256-bit key, on 16-byte blocks. Only the AES cipher direction is needed, since CTR decryption and encryption are the same XOR with the encrypted counter.

The 16-byte counter block is built so it can be found from the address alone: bytes 0 to 7 are a 64-bit nonce held in configuration registers, the same for every block; bytes 8 to 11 are zero; bytes 12 to 15 come from the offset into the encrypted range with its four low bits dropped and four zero bits above. The first 16 bytes of the range use 0, the next 16 use 1, and so on; the offset's four low bits pick the byte of the encrypted counter. The scheme covers up to 4 GB.

An auto-mode read is a sequence of instruction, address, extra byte, dummy clocks and read data phases, set in QSPIC_BURSTCMDA_REG and QSPIC_BURSTCMDB_REG. QSPIC_INST is the instruction for single reads and incrementing bursts; with QSPIC_WRAP_MD = 1, QSPIC_INST_WB is used for a wrapping burst of the length and size in QSPIC_WRAP_LEN and QSPIC_WRAP_SIZE. QSPIC_INST_MD = 1 sends the instruction only on the first access after auto mode is entered (continuous read). QSPIC_EXT_BYTE_EN enables the extra byte, whose value is QSPIC_EXT_BYTE; QSPIC_EXT_HF_DS = 1 floats the pads for its low nibble. QSPIC_DMY_NUM sets the dummy bytes, enabled by QSPIC_DMY_FORCE. Each phase has its own bus width (QSPIC_INST_TX_MD, QSPIC_ADR_TX_MD, QSPIC_EXT_TX_MD, QSPIC_DMY_TX_MD, QSPIC_DAT_RX_MD); if any phase is quad, QSPIC_IO2_OEN and QSPIC_IO3_OEN are written 0. Any instruction other than a read needs manual mode. QSPIC_AUTO_MD = 1 enables auto mode.

With QSPIC_AUTO_MD = 0 the bus is run through QSPIC_CTRLBUS_REG: QSPIC_EN_CS and QSPIC_DIS_CS start and end an access, and the width is set by one of QSPIC_SET_QUAD, QSPIC_SET_DUAL or QSPIC_SET_SINGLE. A write to QSPIC_WRITEDATA sends data, a read of QSPIC_READDATA receives, a write to QSPIC_DUMMYDATA sends dummy clocks. If those accesses are slow because of AHB latency, QSPIC_HRDY_MD = 1 lets every bus master carry on without waiting for the SPI transfer; software then polls QSPIC_BUSY before the next access and reads a received word from QSPIC_RECVDATA. QSPIC_IO3_OEN/QSPIC_IO3_DAT and QSPIC_IO2_OEN/QSPIC_IO2_DAT set the state of IO3 and IO2 for the write-protect and hold functions.

operation.topic: QSPI flash clock and read sampling
operation.text: QSPIC_CLK_MD selects SPI mode 0 (QSPI_SCK low when idle, QSPI_CS high) or mode 3 (QSPI_SCK high when idle). QSPI_CLK is XTAL32M or the PLL divided by 1, 2, 4 or 8 in CLK_AMBA_REG[QSPI_DIV], and may be faster or slower than HCLK. Read data is normally sampled on the rising edge of QSPI_SCK; for a flash with a long output delay QSPIC_RXD_NEG samples on the falling edge, QSPI_RPIPE_EN = 1 pipelines the received data and QSPI_PCLK_MD delays the sampling clock. At VDD = 0.9 V (POWER_CTRL_REG[VDD_LEVEL] = 0x0) with QSPI_CLK = 32 MHz, QSPIC_CTRLMODE_REG[QSPIC_PCLK_MD] is set to 2; at VDD = 1.2 V it is set to 7.

Present on DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699; DA14691 does not have it. QSPIC2 connects a serial flash or a serial RAM (PSRAM) over single, dual or quad SPI, master only, clock modes 0 and 3, up to 96 MHz, giving cheap extra RAM for data used rarely. In auto mode up to 32 MB is memory mapped for reads and writes with 3-byte or 4-byte addressing; in manual mode the register file drives the bus. It has a vendor independent instruction sequencer, fully programmable flash control in auto mode, a special instruction for a programmable wrapping burst, and erase suspend/resume. Its clock QSPIR_CLK, 96 MHz at most, comes through the QSPIC2_DIV divider; its pins are QSPIR_CLK on P0_05, QSPIR_CS on P0_04 and QSPI2_IO0 to IO3 on P0_00 to P0_03, in the V18P supply domain.

operation.topic: QSPI RAM/flash controller signals and modes
operation.text: Signals and bus widths are those of the flash controller: QSPI_SCK, active-low QSPI_CS, IO0 and IO1 as data out and in in single mode, IO2 (WPn) and IO3 (HOLDn) as general purpose outputs in single mode, all four bidirectional in quad. The single mode has no bus modes 1 and 2, no full duplex and no slave mode. Auto and manual mode exclude each other; the mode registers can be written at any time. QSPIC2_USE_32BA = 0 reaches 16 MB with 3-byte addresses, 1 reaches 32 MB with 4-byte addresses.

operation.topic: QSPI RAM/flash controller auto mode access
operation.text: With QSPIC2_AUTO_MD = 0 accesses to the mapped space are ignored. With a flash (QSPIC2_SRAM_EN = 0) only reads are served, transparently, as single, incrementing or wrapping bursts, and a write causes a CPU hard fault. With a serial RAM (QSPIC2_SRAM_EN = 1 and QSPIC2_AUTO_MD = 1) reads work the same way and writes of every burst kind are turned into QSPI write commands; throughput depends on burst length, word width, the memory's protocol overhead and the QSPI clock, and is highest for bursts. Manual mode works as on the flash controller with 8, 16 and 32-bit accesses. Byte order is little-endian.

The same seven-state erase, suspend and resume machine as the flash controller runs when a flash is attached (QSPIC2_SRAM_EN = 0), with QSPIC2_-prefixed registers; on this controller QSPIC2_RESSUS_DLY runs on a 288 kHz clock and QSPIC2_RESSTS_DLY on the SPI clock, chosen by QSPIC2_STSDLY_SEL. Since QSPI_RESSTS_DLY is counted in QSPI_CLK cycles, it is checked against the flash's timing before QSPI_CLK is changed.

operation.topic: QSPI flash programming and low power
operation.text: Programming flash sectors is done in manual mode, polling the flash status bit, with the CPU running from RAM and interrupts disabled during the write command; byte programs are short enough for a polling loop. For least power the QSPI clock is kept as fast as possible so bursts are short, and the CPU as slow as possible. With a slow CPU (for example 2 MHz) and a fast QSPI clock (for example 32 MHz), QSPIC2_CTRLMODE_REG[QSPIC2_FORCENSEQ_EN] = 1 selects split bursts: each word is fetched as its own address/extra/dummy/data access with QSPI_CS going high between them, so the flash is deselected once each access is done. With 0, a burst keeps QSPI_CS low throughout for highest performance.

operation.topic: QSPI RAM/flash controller auto mode setup
operation.text: In auto mode the controller executes from address 0 through the CPU remap function. Some PSRAMs (for example APmemory APS3204J) limit how long CE# may stay low (tCEM), so the QSPI clock must not run too slow during a burst or data may be lost. Read bursts are set in QSPIC2_BURSTCMDA_REG and QSPIC2_BURSTCMDB_REG exactly as on the flash controller (QSPIC2_INST, QSPIC2_INST_WB with QSPIC2_WRAP_MD, QSPIC2_INST_MD, extra byte, QSPIC2_DMY_NUM, per-phase bus widths, IO2/IO3 output enables cleared for quad). Write bursts to a PSRAM (QSPIC2_AUTO_MD = 1, QSPIC2_SRAM_EN = 1) have instruction, address, extra byte and write data phases set in QSPIC2_AWRITECMD_REG: QSPIC2_WR_INST is the write instruction for every burst kind, and QSPIC2_WR_INST_TX_MD, QSPIC2_WR_ADR_TX_MD and QSPIC2_WR_DAT_TX_MD set the bus widths. A RAM needing a special command sequence before writes is prepared in manual mode.

operation.topic: QSPI RAM/flash controller manual mode, clock and sampling
operation.text: Manual mode uses QSPIC2_CTRLBUS_REG, QSPIC2_WRITEDATA, QSPIC2_READDATA and QSPIC2_DUMMYDATA as on the flash controller; during dummy clocks the IO pads are high impedance. QSPIC2_HRDY_MD = 1 keeps the slave's hready at 1 for those registers so masters need not wait; QSPIC2_BUSY is then read before the next access and QSPIC2_RECVDATA holds the received word. QSPIC2_CLK_MD selects mode 0 or mode 3. The clock is XTAL or the PLL divided by 1, 2, 4 or 8 in CLK_AMBA_REG[QSPIC2_DIV]. QSPIC2_RXD_NEG samples on the falling edge; QSPI_RPIPE_EN and QSPI_PCLK_MD pipeline and delay the sampling. At VDD = 0.9 V with QSPI_CLK = 32 MHz QSPIC_PCLK_MD is 2; at VDD = 1.2 V it is 7.

Present on DA14699 only; DA14691, DA14695 and DA14697 do not have it. The motor controller drives the stepping (Lavet) motors of watch hands forward or back: up to five hands, each through up to four GPIOs. Up to 64 commands sit in a memory mapped FIFO and the waveforms in a 48-place register memory holding up to 12 wave definitions (fewer for longer waves). Waveform slots have 30.5 µs granularity. Five independent four-signal pattern generators drive signals singly, in pairs or as a quad. The command read pointer is kept in retained registers, and the CPU is prompted to save the last movement to external non-volatile memory. Triggers are the CPU, a divided sleep clock or a programmable RTC event. It interrupts the CPU on FIFO underrun or overflow. It runs on pclk and makes patterns from the sleep clock, which must be slower than pclk.

Each pattern generator is a state machine making the four signal waveforms for one hand. The command FIFO and wave register file combine queued commands with wave definitions. An interrupt generator and the AHB configuration and control registers complete the block. The command FIFO is 64 words of 16 bits, readable as memory and written at one address. It runs in run-through mode (the read pointer advances until the FIFO is empty) or cyclic mode (it wraps after a programmable position, at most 63).

operation.topic: Step motor waveform timing and triggers
operation.text: A slot is set in five bits from 30.5 µs (one sleep-clock period, value 0) to 32 × 30.5 µs = 976 µs. The longest waveform is 47 ToDs of 32 slots each, 1468 ms in all; the shortest is 3 ToDs of one slot, 90 µs. Each trigger pops commands from the FIFO: a self-clearing software register bit, a tick from the sleep clock divided by up to 64 (about a 1 ms period), or an RTC event settable in multiples of 10 ms. One or more commands are read per trigger according to N_CMDs, on sys_clk; waves are generated on mc_clk, the low power clock divided by MC_CLK_DIV. The FIFO read pointer is made of retention flip-flops, keeps its value when the motor controller's power domain is off, and is cleared only by power-on reset, not by a hardware reset such as a brown-out. Both pointers are readable. Waves are loaded through WAVETABLE_BASE in 5-bit chunks, four per 32-bit write, each chunk a PuN or ToD; the first write is at 0x50030E40, the second at 0x50030E44, the twelfth at 0x50030E6C.

Every pattern generator watches the FIFO output and acts only on commands with its PG_ID; the addressed one stores the wave start index and begins, or waits until one or more of its signals have received commands. MoI (motor idle) is a 10-bit count of slots, 0 allowed, added after every command and shared by all five generators. In mirroring mode one signal repeats another's wave, or one pair repeats the other pair's, after MoI. While a generator is producing a wave it is busy: further commands for it are discarded until it finishes, while commands for other generators still go out.

An interrupt is raised when a generator starts a waveform (rising edge of its busy signal; this source is off during hand animations) and when the read pointer minus the write pointer falls below a programmable threshold of commands left. The start interrupt lets the CPU save the read pointer in flash so that after a power failure the hand can be returned to its last position; the time to write and read the flash relative to the tick period sets how large the one-tick error can be.

Setup order: choose the system clock and the sleep clock in CLK_CTRL_REG (SYS_CLK_SEL, LP_CLK_SEL); set the slot divider CLK_PER_REG[MC_CLK_DIV]; set the pattern generator GPIOs to Px_yy_MODE_REG[PID] = 43 (PG); enable automatic triggers (in SMOTOR_CTRL_REG, TRIG_RTC_EVENT_EN for the RTC and MC_LP_CLK_TRIG_EN for the divided sleep clock); choose normal or cyclic FIFO (CYCLIC_MODE) and the FIFO threshold (SMOTOR_THRESHOLD); enable the wanted interrupts (threshold, generation start and end, per generator start and end, FIFO underrun and overflow); set each generator's start mode (PGx_CTRL_REG[PG_START_MODE]); load the waves into WAVETABLE_BASE; enable the block with CLK_PER_REG[MC_CLK_EN] and the signals with PGx_CTRL_REG[SIGx_EN]; push commands into SMOTOR_CMD_FIFO_REG; then pop them by hand through SMOTOR_TRIGGER_REG or let the RTC or divided sleep clock trigger them.

Present on DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699; DA14691 does not have it. The LCD controller drives a display over a parallel interface or serial SPI3/SPI4, with one layer, a dedicated DMA engine fetching the image once timing parameters are set, output formatting for the target panel and a programmable interrupt, all set from a global register file.

In the HSYNC/VSYNC parallel interface HSYNC pulses every line and VSYNC every frame; the clock output polarity is selectable and each pulse length programmable. A JDI parallel interface is also supported. Colour data is two bits each of red, green and blue.

The 3-wire interface uses CS, SCLK and DO (MOSI); the 4-wire adds DCS, with DO taken as a command while DCS is low and as data while it is high. SCLK may stop when idle. In 4-wire mode each packet is 8 bits with the command/data flag on DCS; in 3-wire mode each packet is 9 bits, the flag bit followed by the byte. MSB first in both. The active level of CS, the SCLK edge that samples data and the clock polarity are all configurable. If CS stays active after a packet, the MSB of the next byte follows on the next clock edge.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. Eight DMA channels move data between any on-chip RAM and the SPI, UART, I2C, USB, PCM, SRC, SD_ADC and GP_ADC blocks, or memory to memory, interrupting the CPU only after a programmable number of transfers. Peripheral requests are multiplexed onto the channels. Each channel has full 32-bit source and destination pointers, a programmable length, flexible interrupts, an optional peripheral trigger with programmable edge-sensitive requests, a memory-initialise option, AHB bursts of 4 or 8 beats (INCR4, INCR8) for transfers between memories or between memory and peripherals, bus error detection with an interrupt, and freeze, including during a memory-to-memory transfer. Channel 7 can be a secure channel.

DMA_REQ_MUX_REG routes peripheral requests: a peripheral selected in field DMAxy_SEL sends its TX request to channel x and its RX request to channel y, and acknowledges are routed back the same way. If two selector fields hold the same value, the less significant one wins.

DMA_ON starts a channel and clears itself when the transfer ends. With DREQ_MODE = 0 the channel starts at once; with 1 it waits for its peripheral's request. Data moves from DMAx_A_START_REG to DMAx_B_START_REG for DMAx_LEN_REG items of 8, 16 or 32 bits; a 16-bit index DMAx_IDX_REG, cleared at the start and compared with the length after each item, is scaled by AINC, BINC and BW and added to the start addresses. AINC or BINC is 0 when the side is a register. The channel stops when it has done its length, provided DREQ_MODE is 0 or the index has reached DMAx_LEN_REG. CIRCULAR = 1 restarts from the start addresses automatically, except when the channel was started with DREQ_MODE = 0, which always stops. A channel interrupts when DMAx_INT_REG equals the index, after the transfer and before the increment; DMA_x_INT_REG = 0 with DMA_x_LEN_REG = 0 gives one transfer and one interrupt. Nothing guards against wrong register settings, but DMAx_CTRL_REG[BUS_ERROR_DETECT] gives an interrupt on a read or write bus error.

DMA_PRIO[2:0] sets each channel's priority; equal priorities fall back to a fixed order. With DREQ_MODE = 0 a channel with DMA_IDLE set can be interrupted by a higher priority one. With DMA_INIT set the active channel holds the bus until it finishes, whatever DMA_IDLE says; it is meant only for filling a memory block with one value read from memory, with AINC = 0 and BINC = 1, and is 0 for peripheral transfers. The same fill with AINC = 0 and BINC = 1 but without DMA_INIT works if the source value does not change, but may be interrupted by higher priority channels.

Writing 1 to SET_FREEZE_REG[FRZ_DMA] freezes all channels, memory-to-memory transfers included; writing 1 to RESET_FREEZE_REG releases them. If the security flag is set in the OTP header, channel 7 becomes the secure channel and is reserved for carrying keys out of the symmetric key area into the AES engine or into the QSPI flash controller's decryptor, out of the CPU's reach.

Memory to memory: set DMAx_LEN_REG, DMAx_A_START_REG, DMAx_B_START_REG and DMAx_INT_REG, enable the channel interrupt in DMA_INT_MASK_REG if wanted, set AINC, BINC, BW and BURST_MODE in DMAx_CTRL_REG, set DMA_ON, wait for DMA_ON = 0 or the interrupt, and clear it in DMA_INT_STATUS_REG. Peripheral to memory: the source is the peripheral's receive register (for example I2C_DATA_CMD_REG) with AINC off, the peripheral is mapped to the channel pair in DMA_REQ_MUX_REG[DMAxy_SEL], DREQ_MODE and DMA_PRIO are set, then DMA_ON, then the peripheral's own DMA request is enabled (for example I2C_DMA_CR_REG[TDMAE]). SPI does not support burst transfers.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. The AES/HASH engine accelerates the algorithms needed for RFC4835: AES with 128, 192 or 256-bit keys in ECB, CBC and CTR modes, and the hashes MD5, SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, with HMAC-SHA-256. Its own AHB master DMA moves data to and from shared memory through RX and TX FIFOs, in bursts; its registers sit on an AHB slave. Input can be fragmented, the internal DMA being programmed once for each fragment in turn.

AES follows FIPS PUB 197, on 128-bit blocks. Padding to a multiple of 16 bytes for AES is left to software. Repeated AES-CBC encryptions in software give HMAC-XCBC-AES-96; AES-CCM can be built with AES-CBC giving the authentication and AES-CTR the encryption. Hash input is padded in hardware to a multiple of 512 or 1024 bits: a 0x80 byte after the data, zero bytes until the length mod 512/1024 is 448/896, then the message length in bits as a 64/128-bit big-endian number; the FIFOs switch to 8-byte mode meanwhile. The 128 to 512-bit result goes out in 64-byte blocks. MD5 follows RFC1321; SHA-1, SHA-224/256 and SHA-384/512 follow FIPS PUB 180-4.

AES: set CLK_AMBA_REG[AES_CLK_ENABLE]; CRYPTO_CTRL_REG[CRYPTO_HASH_SEL] = 0; choose the mode in CRYPTO_ALG_MD (the IV or counter block for CBC/CTR goes in CRYPTO_MREGx_REG), the algorithm in CRYPTO_ALG and the key size in CRYPTO_AES_KEY_SZ; with key expansion (CRYPTO_AES_KEXP) the base key goes in CRYPTO_KEYS_START memory; set CRYPTO_FETCH_ADDR_REG, CRYPTO_DEST_ADDR_REG, CRYPTO_LEN_REG and CRYPTO_ENCDEC; start with CRYPTO_START_REG[CRYPTO_START] and wait for CRYPTO_STATUS_REG[CRYPTO_INACTIVE] = 1. Hash: the same with CRYPTO_HASH_SEL = 1, CRYPTO_HASH_OUT_LEN setting how many result bytes the DMA writes, and no key or direction. CRYPTO_IRQ_EN gives an interrupt on completion. The clock is switched off again after each operation when nothing else is queued.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. The TRNG supplies seeds for encryption; its output can be the entropy input of a FIPS 140-2 approved deterministic generator run in software with the hardware accelerators, optionally NIST SP800-90A Hash_DRBG with SHA-256. Ring oscillators of inverters drive a flip-flop into metastability; their output is whitened in a shift register and stored in a 32 by 32-bit FIFO read over AHB, with registers on APB32 and its own TRNG_IRQ. The oscillators run only with TRNG_CTRL_REG[TRNG_ENABLE] = 1 and room left in the FIFO. Each 32 random bits take 512 pclk cycles, so a full FIFO takes 16K cycles, 500 µs at 32 MHz. Use: set CLK_AMBA_REG[TRNG_CLK_EN], set TRNG_ENABLE (ignored while the FIFO is full), poll TRNG_FIFOLVL_REG or wait for TRNG_IRQ, read the numbers at 0x30050000 (TRNG_M), then clear both bits to save power; the FIFO is readable only while TRNG_CLK_EN = 1. Data is little-endian.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. The wake-up controller wakes the chip from extended or deep sleep (clocked) and from hibernation (clockless). It watches any GPIO for a change, with polarity set per pin, latches what it sees, raises three interrupts to the Cortex-M33 and passes the PDC a bus showing which GPIO toggled. It has two parallel circuits.

KEY_WAKEUP watches chosen GPIOs for an edge or level and can debounce a key press for 0 to 63 ms before raising KEY_WKUP_GPIO_IRQ to the M33 and the PDC (where it is called Debounced_IO). With debounce 0 it fires on the edge, but the input must stay asserted at least 2 RC32K periods while the system is active, or 4 RC32K periods in hibernation. It wakes from hibernation as well as deep and extended sleep, and is the only circuit that can wake from hibernation since it starts the RC32K oscillator. The interrupt stays asserted until software acknowledges it, so the M33 sees it once the PDC (with a matching entry) has powered it. When several GPIOs toggled it does not say which.

GPIO_WAKEUP latches rising or falling edges into a status register, so the source is known; the status goes to the PDC as trigger signals, and an OR of each port forms the level interrupts GPIO_P0_IRQ and GPIO_P1_IRQ to the M33 (pulses at least 2 RC32K periods). It wakes from deep or extended sleep but not hibernation; the interrupts stay asserted until acknowledged. Setup: CLK_TMR_REG[WAKEUPCT_ENABLE]; polarity in WKUP_POL_Px_REG; debounce in WKUP_CTRL_REG[WKUP_DEB_VALUE]; PDC entries for sleep; clear latches in WKUP_CLEAR_Px_REG; wake-up events in WKUP_SELECT_Px_REG; GPIO interrupts in WKUP_SEL_GPIO_Px_REG; then enable whichever of the interrupts KEY_WKUP_GPIO_IRQn, PDC_IRQn, GPIO_P0_IRQn and GPIO_P1_IRQn are used.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. The GPADC is a 10-bit dynamic SAR converter: 125 ns conversion, up to 4 Msample/s, 13 µA typical at 100 ksample/s. It measures single-ended or differential, in two ranges through a 3x attenuator, on eight single-ended inputs on VFBGA100 (four on VFBGA86) or four differential pairs on both packages. Oversampling up to 128 times gives up to 11.2 effective bits. It also has battery monitoring, chopping, offset and zero-scale adjustment, common-mode adjustment and DMA. Its own 1.2 V LDO is the full-scale reference.

The analog part runs from an internal 100 MHz oscillator by default, or from ADC_CLK, as the GP_ADC_CLK_SEL bit of GP_ADC_CTRL_REG selects; the logic runs on ADC_CLK, 16 MHz or 96 MHz per CLK_PER_REG[GPADC_CLK_SEL]. A high-PSRR 1.2 V reference LDO is enabled by GP_ADC_CTRL_REG[GP_ADC_EN]. A 1.2 V digital LDO, switched by the LDO_VDDD_HIGH_ENABLE bit of GP_ADC_CTRL_REG, is fed from V18P, which must be on before the GPADC is used. Registers GP_ADC_* sit on APB; the block has a maskable ADC_IRQ and a DMA request. The input selector reaches up to eight GPIOs, the battery voltage and analog ground. Other inputs are VDD (the 0.9/1.2 V core rail), V30, VSSA and the die temperature sensor. Internal 80 kΩ and 160 kΩ resistors form the 3x attenuator. The VBAT scaler maps 5 V to 1.2 V, so one LSB is 5 / 1023 = 4.88 mV. With GP_ADC_CTRL2_REG[GP_ADC_ATTN3X] = 1, inputs up to 3.45 V can be measured.

The ADC runs in manual or continuous mode, either one optionally with oversampling or chopping. Setting GP_ADC_CTRL_REG[GP_ADC_EN] turns on the LDO first; the ADC is ready after the GP_ADC_EN_DEL count in GP_ADC_CTRL3_REG, usually 20 µs of LDO settling. Being dynamic, the ADC draws no static current apart from about 5 µA in its LDO, so GP_ADC_EN is cleared when the ADC is idle. In manual mode GP_ADC_START begins a conversion; when done GP_ADC_START returns to 0, GP_ADC_INT is set and GP_ADC_RESULT_REG holds the value; software checks GP_ADC_START = 0 before the next start. In continuous mode (GP_ADC_CONT = 1) a new conversion starts as each ends, after one GP_ADC_START, and the result register always holds the latest value; it is stopped by clearing GP_ADC_CONT and waiting for GP_ADC_START = 0, which is also required before changing any setting. At full speed the ADC draws about 75 µA; below 100 ksample/s about 13 µA. GP_ADC_CTRL3_REG[GP_ADC_INTERVAL] sets the gap between conversions in 1.024 ms steps; 0 restarts at once, and a non-zero value may delay the first conversion up to 1 ms while it synchronises to the delay clock.

Each conversion samples for GP_ADC_CTRL2_REG[GP_ADC_SMPL_TIME], converts, then stores after GP_ADC_CTRL2_REG[GP_ADC_STORE_DEL]. The sampling time constant depends on the source impedance, the internal dividers and the 0.5 pF sampling capacitor; settling needs about 7 time constants for 10 bits and 9 for 12 bits, counted in units of 32 ADC_CLK cycles. GP_ADC_SMPL_TIME may be 0 when settling takes less than a single ADC_CLK cycle. Example: VBAT with τADC = 500 ns at 32 MHz gives 7 × 500E-9 × 32E6 / 32 = 3.5, so 4. Conversion takes about 125 ns on the internal 100 MHz oscillator. With GP_ADC_STORE_DEL = 0 (handshake) the result is ready after the conversion plus synchronisation: 4 + 3 ADC_CLK cycles at 32 MHz, 12 + 3 at 96 MHz. With GP_ADC_STORE_DEL > 0 (fixed) the result is stored after GP_ADC_STORE_DEL + 1 cycles whether ready or not.

Oversampling averages 2^GP_ADC_CONV_NRS successive conversions; the 16-bit result in GP_ADC_RESULT_REG is left-aligned and gains effective bits with the count. Chopping swaps the inputs and outputs between conversions to cancel the ADC's own offset and smooth other errors, suited to DC and slow signals; it works in manual, continuous and oversampling modes, taking two samples of opposite sign, or an even number set by GP_ADC_CONV_NRS when oversampling. GP_ADC_CTRL_REG[GP_ADC_CHOP] enables it. The natural zero of the ADC is mid-scale (511.5, 0x1FF/0x200), ideally 0.6 V single-ended and 0 V differential; with GP_ADC_ATTN3X = 1 it is 1.8 V single-ended and 0 V differential. GP_ADC_MUTE = 1 connects the input to mid-scale, so the result shows the offset (515 means +3.5). GP_ADC_SIGN = 1 inverts input and output, flipping the offset's sign (508 with the same offset); the two results add to 1023, the mid-scale of an 11-bit word, whose LSB is dropped for a 10-bit result (511 or 512).

Besides DNL and INL the ADC has a linear gain error, which slightly changes the effective range, and a linear offset error, which shifts it off centre; offset is reduced by chopping or calibration. With a noise-free input the noise averages ±1 LSB, and averaging more samples (GP_ADC_CONV_NRS) lowers it. With a clean input (a filter capacitor close to the pin) most noise comes from the ADC's LDO, which has no pin for a capacitor. GP_ADC_I20U = 1 puts a constant 20 µA load on the LDO so its current never drops to zero, and GP_ADC_IDYN = 1 adds 10 µA during sampling so the load matches the conversion phase.

The small dynamic comparator gives an offset of up to 20 mV (about 20 LSB). Chopping cancels it but it still causes saturation near zero and full scale; The two offset registers (OFFP and OFFN) compensate it inside the ADC network. Calibration is recommended at initialisation; accuracy improves with a sampling time setting of 2 or 3 and a conversion count setting of 3 or 4, and is verified by a result near 0x200 with GP_ADC_MUTE = 1. The same registers can set the zero-scale or full-scale point, for example 0x000 at exactly 0.0 V, or a sensor's zero. A differential signal's common mode should be 0.6 V (1.8 V with GP_ADC_ATTN3X = 1), with up to 50 mV margin; otherwise the registers shift the ADC's common mode, and offset calibration can be combined by replacing 0x200 with the common-mode value. With a common mode below 0.5 V or above 0.7 V the input no longer covers the whole range.

There is no input buffer. During sampling a 0.5 pF capacitor, precharged to mid-scale, is switched onto the input, so the static input impedance is infinite; 10-bit accuracy needs at least seven time constants of source impedance, internal dividers and the 0.5 pF. Source-to-pin inductance has to be kept very low; if it is not, filter capacitors go from the pins to ground (single-ended) or across the pins (differential). With GP_ADC_MUTE = 1 the internal noise should average under ±2 LSB; more noise on an input channel is reduced with external filter capacitors.

The GPADC reads every on-chip temperature sensor. The charger's sensor gives a fairly accurate die temperature: GP_ADC_DIFF_TEMP_EN = 0, GP_ADC_SEL = 20, GP_ADC_DIFF_TEMP_SEL = 2. Three simple diode sensors, beside the radio, the charger and the bandgap, give relative readings only: GP_ADC_DIFF_TEMP_EN = 1, GP_ADC_SEL = 20, GP_ADC_DIFF_TEMP_SEL picks the sensor. Power dissipation is kept constant while measuring or calibrating, since internal thermal gradients shift the reading. Setup of a conversion: GP_ADC_EN; the GPIO as Px_yy_MODE_REG[PID] = 26; GP_ADC_SEL; GP_ADC_SE; GP_ADC_CONT; other options in GP_ADC_CTRLx_REG; GP_ADC_START; wait for GP_ADC_START = 0 or the interrupt; clear it by writing GP_ADC_CLEAR_INT_REG; read GP_ADC_RESULT_REG.

Present on DA14691, DA14695, DA14697 and DA14699. A second-order 14-bit sigma-delta ADC converts in about 1 ms, so up to 1000 samples per second. The reference is the internal 1.2 V (default) or an external one. It measures single-ended or differential in two input scales: eight single-ended inputs on VFBGA100 (four on VFBGA86) or four differential pairs on VFBGA100 (two on VFBGA86), plus a separate VBAT input read through an internal 160 kΩ and 3 × 160 kΩ divider. Results can go out by the general DMA. The analog part is the modulator with an 8-input mux and a reference selector; it reaches 14 bits at its thermal noise floor, and single-shot readings need a higher oversampling ratio than continuous operation because of the step response. The digital part holds the filter and control, runs the chopping and dynamic element matching, and drives the muxes.
